newsitem.title: USA: BP to boost Alaska investment by $1 billion.
newsitem.headline: BP to boost Alaska investment by $1 billion.

text.p: BP Exploration Alaska Inc., a unit of British Petroleum Co. Plc, said Monday it planned to increase its capital spending in Alaska by $1 billion over the next five years and reverse the slide in oil production from the state's North Slope.
The company's yearly outlay will rise to an average of $700 million from $500 million, BP Alaska President John Morgan and Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles told a news conference.
Total capital spending will rise to $3.5 billion over the next five years from $2.5 billion.
The increased investment is part of a strategy to boost BP's worldwide oil production to 1.8 million barrels a day by 2000 from the current rate of 1.5 million barrels a day, Morgan said.

In Alaska, BP expects to boost its share of North Slope production to nearly 600,000 barrels a day by 2002 from the current rate of 525,000 barrels a day -- a reversal of fortune from the "slow decline" considered inevitable two years ago, Morgan said.
"I think it's a story now of a very healthy future for the industry in Alaska," he said.
The total spending of $3.5 billion will include $1.2 billion for enhanced-recovery projects and development drilling and $1.5 billion for Northstar, Badami and other new fields, Morgan said.
BP seeks ultimately to add 4 billion to 5 billion barrels in recoverable oil reserves over the next decade, Morgan said.

That figure does not include possible development in the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska, a federally owned reserve west of Prudhoe Bay, or in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge east of Prudhoe Bay, Morgan said.

Accompanying the new investment will be some production job cuts because of an impending "restructuring" at Prudhoe Bay, North America's largest oil field and the backbone of all North Slope operations, and other old fields, Morgan said.

Prudhoe production is down to about 830,000 barrels a day, from its 1.5 million barrel peak in the late 1980s, and is forecast to drop to 500,000 to 600,000 barrels a day in three years, despite the enhanced recovery projects there, he said.

New sources of oil will be "less manpower-intensive" than Prudhoe and other old fields, Morgan said. But Prudhoe job cuts were likely to be more than offset by new jobs related to the company's growth, he added.
Knowles, just returned from a trade mission to BP's worldwide headquarters in Britain, hailed the investment announcement.
"This is great news. It does certainly show that we are open and ready for business," the governor, a Democrat, said.

Despite the potential of reversing the North Slope production decline, Alaska Natural Resources Commissioner John Shively, also attending the news conference, warned that Alaska was not on the verge of another 1970s-style oil boom.
"It's not quite time to burst out in another refrain of 'Happy Days are Here Again,' because it's not the late 1970s," said Shively, referring to the early days of North Slope production.
Production of Alaska North Slope crude has dropped to about 1.4 million barrels per day from over 2 million barrels a day in 1988.
More than half of all North Slope production projected by the year 2000 depends on investments yet to be made, Knowles said.
